title: Glowsea is on iOS — making a jellyfish's light part of the stealth rules
author: Training_Relation_89
selftext:
We publish Glowsea, a stealth-and-rescue adventure about a jellyfish searching for lost companions. Swimming makes you shine and draws attention; releasing the controls lets you dim and hide. The same light that helps you find your way can give you away.

AI tools assisted the code, artwork and text. One lesson from developing it has been that a working mechanic isn't the same as a readable encounter. A tester found that waiting out a watcher felt too safe. The opening was revised to offer a route around cover and a shorter route tied to a guard's calm state, rather than simply making every enemy faster. That feedback was useful even though the exact original encounter wasn't identified.

Later chapters change the problem: currents carry decoys, wreck corridors constrain escapes, and cold areas ask you to connect warmth stations. Enemy reactions follow authored game rules; there is no live AI chat or model running the characters during play. Those encounters still need real play checks—AI-generated code and a passing build don't prove the timing feels fair.

The first chapter (levels 1–7) is free to play in your browser, with no account or download: https://games.shapemo.com/play/glowsea/?utm\_source=reddit&utm\_medium=organic\_social&utm\_campaign=glowsea\_20261120&utm\_content=aigamedev\_release

It is also out on iPhone and iPad. Chapter one is free, with one optional Full Game purchase for the remaining chapters: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/glowsea/id6828685533

If you try the browser opening, we'd welcome the first moment when hiding or a watcher's reaction felt unclear. No need to finish the chapter.

comments.author: Fancy-Proof-9449
comments.body:
Love the core idea: the thing that helps you is also the thing that gives you away. That's a much more interesting stealth rule than a plain visibility meter, because every movement becomes a small risk decision.

"A working mechanic isn't the same as a readable encounter" is so true. The waiting-out-the-watcher fix is a nice example of solving it with level design instead of just turning the difficulty up. Out of curiosity, how do you show the player how bright they are at any moment? With light as the stealth rule, the hardest part is probably making "how visible am I right now" readable at a glance on a small phone screen.

replies.author: Training_Relation_89
replies.body: The jellyfish itself is the main cue: it brightens as you swim and dims when you release and stop. That puts the feedback where you're already looking, though it doesn't by itself tell you whether a particular watcher can see you. You're right that phone-scale readability is a separate thing to check; I wouldn't claim the glow alone proves that part is clear.
